brief.subject: Diesel falls 19.0 cents as holiday capacity starts to tighten
brief.headline: Diesel slides to $5.937 while pre-Thanksgiving freight tightens and LA-Long Beach avoids a strike
brief.dek: Fuel relief continues, tender rejections may climb into the holiday, a port strike threat eases, and broker liability law keeps shifting.
brief.lede: Diesel fell 19.0 cents to $5.937 a gallon just as early data points to a tightening market ahead of Thanksgiving. Lower fuel and firmer demand could widen margins this week.

sections.heading: Diesel keeps sliding
bullets: $5.937 per gallon: the U.S. average retail diesel price for the week of 2026-11-16.
Down 19.0 cents (3.1%) from the prior week, a meaningful cut to per-mile fuel costs.
Down 33.9 cents over four weeks, so check whether fuel surcharge tables are lagging the drop.

sections.heading: Holiday capacity is tightening
bullets: Tender rejections could top 14% before Thanksgiving, according to a SONAR-based outlook, as low inventories spur last-minute shipping.
That forecast points to stronger spot leverage for carriers with open trucks during holiday week.
Backup carriers are charging shippers more in tight markets, so contingency freight should not be priced cheap.

sections.heading: Port strike threat eases
bullets: A tentative union deal averts an immediate strike at the Port of LA-Long Beach, the nation's busiest container complex.
The accord follows more than a year of bargaining, including federally mediated talks.
Drayage and Southern California lanes should avoid a sudden holiday shutdown, though the deal is not yet final.

sections.heading: Broker liability case moves forward
bullets: J.B. Hunt's brokerage won one ruling and lost another in Arizona federal court on Thursday.
The case is becoming a key test of broker liability after the Montgomery vs. Caribe Transport II decision.
Expect brokers to scrutinize carrier vetting more closely as these rulings shape their legal exposure.

sections.heading: Mexico shifts on trucking safety
bullets: 29 agreements on highway security were reached by Mexican trucking groups and authorities after a nationwide strike.
Mexico also added digital compliance requirements for carriers seeking voluntary safety certification.
Cross-border carriers and their Mexican partners should watch for changing paperwork and security conditions.
